lines.text: kingdom of heaven" has no meaning. The poor in spirit to
whom the kingdom of heaven is promised are they who look
forward to the future which God will bring about-though
not, of course, a worldly future, not a brilliant compensation
for all they have lost. No, something quite different, some-
thing which transcends the things of this world: "What no
eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man conceived,
what God has prepared for those who love Him."
The poor in spirit are they who wait upon the Lord; they
who wait for God's future, because they know that here and
now nothing can give them satisfaction, those who by such
an attitude of waiting on God have inwardly freed themselves
from their attachment to the here and now; such stand in an
attitude of waiting which silences all desires.
Blessed are they who wait! This is also the meaning of the
second beatitude: "Blessed are those who mourn, for they
shall be comforted." Yes, this is the message which we are
to-day most eager to relate to our own position. But again it
is not sorrow as such to which God's message of healing and
deliverance applies; it is a question of understanding rightly
the meaning of this word. All sorrow and pain is intended to
make us aware how insecure is the ground on which we
stand; in every individual case of distress and pain there is
but manifested the deep underlying world agony which
envelops humanity as a whole. In every loss that we suffer
we see the evidence of that power making for transience, the
power of death to which we are all subject. Do we under-
stand our sorrows in this light? For the most part they strike
us as something strange and offensive, astonishing and
frightening. We say, bewildered, "No, that cannot be!" and
fail to recognize that it is but the common human lot. In
spite of all that is beautiful and uplifting, human life, as the
ancient poet Pindar says, is but a shadowy dream. We go
our way as over a surface of ice, which at any moment may
break.
